description: Soy estudiante de tecnología en Colombia, apasionado por el desarrollo de software, la ciberseguridad y la gestión de bases de datos. Tengo experiencia trabajando con integración de APIs, análisis de datos y entornos de sistemas operativos estructurados. Actualmente nuestro equipo ya está conformado en su totalidad para este hackathon, listos para enfocarnos en retos de alto impacto técnico. ¡Les deseamos muchos éxitos a todos los demás participantes en sus proyectos!
summary:
SARitmo is an interactive web app that uses real NISAR radar data from NASA and ISRO to show what changed on Earth's surface between two satellite passes. NISAR returns to the same place every 12 days, so we treat each pass as a note: the timeline is a musical score, and an animation plays every pass in a series while each note sounds at a pitch tied to the strength of the radar return.

Four guided stories teach how to read the data: wetlands in La Mojana (Colombia), farm fields in California's San Joaquin Valley, summer melt on Iceland's Vatnajökull ice cap, and interferograms over the island of Hawaii. Explore mode opens the same workflow for any place NISAR has imaged: search a city, pick two dates, and the app maps where radar return rose or fell, measures each change class in km² and explains the physical hypothesis behind it, with other possible causes.

L-band radar sees through clouds and at night, but radar images are hard to read without training. SARitmo makes NISAR's open data usable by students, journalists and local planners, in English and Spanish. Every class is labelled "possible", and sources, method and validation are one click away.

The Project link is a live copy on Render's free plan, so the first load can take a minute and it runs slower than locally. The full source code is on GitHub: https://github.com/Gxxrazn21/compas-nisar
details:
LIVE APP AND SOURCE CODE

The Project link opens a live copy of SARitmo at https://compas-nisar.onrender.com, hosted on Render's free plan. The free server goes to sleep when nobody is using it, so the first visit can take a minute or more to start, and the app runs slower than on a local computer because the free plan has very limited CPU and memory. The demo video was recorded from the app running locally.

The complete source code, with instructions to run SARitmo locally at full speed, is on GitHub: https://github.com/Gxxrazn21/compas-nisar. It is also listed under Space Agency Partner & Other Data.

WHAT IT DOES

SARitmo opens on a globe with four guided stories built on real NISAR acquisitions from 2026:

• La Mojana, Colombia: wetlands between June and October.

• San Joaquin Valley, United States: farm fields from summer to harvest.

• Vatnajökull, Iceland: summer melt on the ice cap.

• Island of Hawaii, United States: interferograms over the island.

Each story uses the same layers: Before, After, a draggable Curtain to compare both dates, HH change, HV change, Signals and Composite. Beyond the stories, the app offers:

• Explore. Click anywhere on the globe, or search for a city or address. The app queries NASA's catalog, lists the series of passes that cover that point and compares any two dates.

• Reading the change. A map of where radar return rose or fell, change classes with their area in km², a point probe, a histogram, data provenance and the limits of the analysis.

• Why it changed. Each change class comes with its physical hypothesis, other possible causes and the polarization that reveals it.

• The dance. A color animation of every pass in a series (lilac where HH dominates, green where HV dominates) while the score keeps the beat. Each note sounds at its displayed pitch: the stronger the radar return, the higher the note.

• Calibrated lens. With a free Earthdata token, the app reads a window of the full GCOV science product from NASA's cloud and computes change from calibrated values.

• Context. One-click NASA layers: surface water seen by Sentinel-1 (a second radar, in C band), land cover and population density.

• Live. Recent natural events from NASA EONET and the latest NISAR urgent response acquisitions, each one click away from the radar passes over that place. "NISAR now" shows the satellite in 3D at its current position, with its radar swath and its next orbit.

• Tour. A guided tour of about 8.5 minutes and 31 steps covers the satellite, the radar, the data and the app. The app performs each action as the tour explains it.

• Evidence record. In the saved La Mojana walkthrough, the user can check the result against the Sentinel-1 water layer, record agreement or disagreement, add a local reference and export a JSON file or a printable HTML report.

The interface is available in English and Spanish, works on mobile, has keyboard shortcuts and gives every view a permanent link.

HOW IT WORKS

A FastAPI backend queries NASA's Common Metadata Repository (CMR) for NISAR granules and fetches the browse images that the ASF DAAC publishes with each GCOV product. Those previews are not calibrated. Each one is clipped to its own 5th and 95th percentiles and gamma-corrected with an exponent of 0.5, which we confirmed in the nisarqa source code and in each product's quality-control metadata. Two dates therefore cannot be subtracted directly. SARitmo does this instead:

1) Reverses the gamma correction to recover a quantity proportional to power.

2) Smooths speckle with a 5x5-pixel mean.

3) Fits one date to the other's scale with robust reduced major axis regression over unsaturated pixels.

4) Clips both dates to the interval where both hold information.

5) Computes the change in approximate decibels and classifies it with a 3 dB threshold.

The result is change relative to the scene as a whole, not a calibrated value. The app says "approximate dB" and labels every class "possible". It reports fit quality, data coverage and interpretation support separately, because a good fit does not confirm a flood.

The calibrated lens skips the global fit. It reads gamma-nought from the GCOV HDF5 product (10 m, averaged in power to 30 m cells in the La Mojana case) and computes 10 x log10 of the ratio between the two dates. The "possible flooded vegetation" class, for example, requires HH to rise by at least 3 dB while HV stays within 1.5 dB, and an HH return that was not dark before the change.

VALIDATION AND LIMITS

We compared the browse-based change against the calibrated product. In the main 15 km window in La Mojana (June 26 to October 24, 2026; 7,744 common pixels), HH change at the 3 dB threshold gives:

• At about 170 m: correlation 0.517, median absolute error 0.78 dB, precision 50.0%, recall 12.2%.

• With an additional 5x5 mean (about 1 km): correlation 0.861, median absolute error 0.69 dB, precision 12.5%, recall 45.0%.

Correlation is not detection accuracy, the calibrated product is not ground truth, and the physical classes still lack independent validation. The full results and a reproducible JSON file are in the repository (docs/validacion-ampliada.md).

SARitmo does not confirm floods, fires, deforestation or ground deformation. It shows where radar return changed and what that change is consistent with. It is not an alert system. It only compares dates acquired in the same mode, and it shows interferograms as published, without claiming to measure deformation.

BENEFITS

• People with no radar training can ask "what changed here?" of NISAR data and get an answer that comes with its uncertainty.

• Every comparison names both source products, so anyone can look them up in ASF Data Search and check the result.

• The whole interface, including the tour, is in English and Spanish.

• No synthetic data are used. Everything on screen comes from the services listed under NASA Data and Space Agency Partner & Other Data.

• The code is open source under the MIT license, with tests and scripts that reproduce the validation.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

We want NISAR's open data to reach people outside the radar community: students, journalists, local planners and anyone curious about a place they know. The next steps are to test the app with non-specialist users and to check the change classes against field evidence, starting with La Mojana.

TOOLS

• Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn, httpx, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, h5py and pyproj.

• Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, three.js for the 3D model of NISAR, satellite.js for SGP4 orbit propagation, and Vitest for tests.

• Video: Playwright with Google Chrome to record the real app, ffmpeg, a Python script that synthesizes the background track, and the Kokoro text-to-speech model for the voice-over.

• Coding assistants: OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

HOW TO RUN IT

Clone the repository and run scripts\start.ps1 (Python 3.11 or later and Node.js 20 or later). The app opens at http://127.0.0.1:8000. Both API keys are optional: without them everything works except the daily Earth image on the cover and the calibrated lens. The saved La Mojana walkthrough (/?demo=mojana) needs no Earthdata account.

USE OF AI

The code and text of this project, including this page, were written with AI coding assistants (OpenAI Codex and Claude Code), directed and reviewed by the team. The assistants did not generate any data: every image, figure and date in the app comes from the NASA and partner services listed below, and each result can be reproduced with the scripts in the repository. The demo video is a recording of the real app; its voice-over is AI-generated with the Kokoro text-to-speech model, as stated on the video's closing card. The banner image on our team page was generated with an AI image tool and carries a visible "AI-generated image" watermark. The 3D model of NISAR is drawn in code from NASA/JPL public-domain reference views, and the background music comes from a synthesis script.
